title: Booted, then suited: Veterans and the making of Putin’s new proto-elite – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR's original dataset on Russia's “Time of Heroes” programme, its regional clones and the 2026 State Duma slate shows the Kremlin swapping technocratic cadre recruitment for war-veteran recruitment — a shift from “make competent people loyal” to “make loyal people competent”. More than 1,300 veterans already hold state posts and up to 50 will enter the Duma, building a long-lived institutional constituency for confrontation with the West that would raise the domestic cost of any post-ceasefire normalisation.

themes.theme: Cadre policy flips from technocrats to khaki

insights.claim: Russian personnel policy has shifted from a “make competent people loyal” model typical of competitive authoritarianism to a “make loyal people competent” logic typical of consolidated dictatorships, with war service treated as proof of ideological loyalty.
insights.so_what: A regime optimising for loyalty over competence degrades policy quality over time — assume worse Russian macro and administrative management, not better, in any multi-year scenario.
insights.quote: away from a “make competent people loyal” model, associated with competitive authoritarianism, to a “make loyal people competent” logic
insights.locator: The paper shows the Kremlin’s integration of war veterans
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: The veteran-focused Time of Heroes programme effectively supplanted the technocrat-oriented School of Governors in 2025, whose next intake was postponed.
insights.so_what: The clearest institutional marker that Russia's technocratic recruitment channel is being closed rather than merely supplemented.
insights.locator: Time of Heroes is run by the Higher School of Public Administration of RANEPA
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Roughly one in six top Russian officials serving in 2024 was a technocrat — nearly three times the share in 2000 — which is the peak that the war-veteran intake is now reversing.
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline for measuring how fast technocratic influence erodes in Russian ministries and state companies.
insights.locator: Szakonyi’s biographical database of 1,578 senior Russian officials
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Between 2017 and 2024 almost 400 people were trained through Sergei Kiriyenko's School of Governors and 52 graduates became heads of regions, showing how quickly a Kremlin cadre programme can restock the regional bench.
insights.so_what: Gives a conversion-rate benchmark for judging how many Time of Heroes veterans will reach governorships over the next 5-10 years.
insights.locator: A more successful approach emerged after
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: The prolonged war eroded Putin's confidence in technocrats — they appeared insufficiently committed and failed on war-critical tasks such as building fortifications in Kursk — and his relationship even with central bank governor Elvira Nabiullina appears to be changing.
insights.so_what: A direct tail risk to Russian monetary-policy credibility: watch Nabiullina's standing as a leading indicator for CBR independence and rouble/inflation management.
insights.locator: Yet the prolonged war in Ukraine may have eroded the confidence
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Because war credentials and loyalty now carry more weight in appointments than expertise, the Russian economy and bureaucracy will gradually lose capacity to manage the mounting pressures the war creates.
insights.so_what: Argues for a slow-burn deterioration in Russian state administrative quality rather than a sudden break — relevant to long-dated Russia-exposure and sanctions-evasion assumptions.
insights.locator: The fashion for technocrats in the Russian government
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Putin publicly returned to the idea of a veteran “new elite” at least 22 times between February 2024 and July 2026, including in unexpected settings such as a municipal leaders' forum and his televised Direct Line.
insights.so_what: The repetition count is evidence this is a structural project with personal presidential ownership, not a PR campaign that can be quietly dropped.
insights.locator: Between February 2024 and July 2026, Putin returned to this idea
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

themes.theme: Time of Heroes: selection funnel and placement pattern

insights.claim: More than 65,000 people applied online to the federal Time of Heroes programme's first two cohorts but just under 170 reached in-person training, an acceptance rate of about 0.26%.
insights.so_what: Quantifies how narrow the elite channel actually is — the programme is a signalling device far more than a mass mobility route.
insights.locator: Official figures show more than 65,000 people applied online
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Hard skills and practical administrative work account for 68% of the Time of Heroes curriculum versus 34% for the School of Governors, while team-building falls to 11% from 35% — evidence the state is teaching competence to people it already trusts.
insights.so_what: Curriculum composition is the hard evidence behind the loyalty-competence thesis; both programmes devote a similar 11-13% to political indoctrination.
insights.locator: Hard skills and practical administrative work account for 68%
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Of the 169 federal Time of Heroes participants, 84% had exclusively military backgrounds, 94% of those assessable had confirmed combat service, almost 40% held major combat decorations and at least 13 have been accused of war crimes.
insights.so_what: Rebuts the early assumption that the programme was a fake credential for careerist officials — the federal cohort is genuinely combat-based, which makes its political durability higher.
insights.locator: Of the participants, 84% have exclusively military backgrounds
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: By July 2026, 108 of 169 federal Time of Heroes participants had been appointed to government or state-company posts, but 85% of those appointments settled in middle and upper-middle ranks and none reached federal minister, agency head or deputy prime minister.
insights.so_what: The veteran wave is a bench being built, not a takeover — its impact lands in 4-6 years as these mid-rankers rise, not now.
insights.locator: By July 2026, 108 of the 169 participants
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Veteran appointments cluster into four functions — management (47-54%), ideology (35% of federal posts), veteran liaison (15-20%) and security liaison — placing war participants in Roscosmos, Rostelecom, the presidential administration and the Central Election Commission.
insights.so_what: Shows exactly which Russian institutions are absorbing war-linked cadres, including state-owned enterprises that Western counterparties still touch indirectly.
insights.locator: Management is the largest category at both federal and regional levels
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: In 88% of cases a veteran's regional appointment was in their home region and in about 45% it matched the institution or region of their programme internship, showing placements run on pre-existing local ties rather than open competition.
insights.so_what: Predicts where the next cohort lands: track regional internships to anticipate appointments.
insights.locator: Veterans’ career trajectories suggest that appointments usually build on existing connections
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: No biographical or service characteristic was a statistically significant predictor of receiving an appointment, which means patronage relationships with supervisors and curators, not merit or heroism, drive subsequent advancement.
insights.so_what: Anyone modelling Russian elite succession should weight patron networks over combat résumés when forecasting who rises.
insights.locator: Yet none of the biographical or service-related characteristics
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

themes.theme: Regional programmes and the demobilisation overhang

insights.claim: Every Russian region except Moscow launched its own Time of Heroes clone during 2025 under a Kremlin requirement to train 30-60 veterans a year, a metric now sitting alongside poverty, healthcare access and demographic targets.
insights.so_what: Turning veteran integration into a governor KPI guarantees mechanical over-compliance and a rapidly growing pool of war-credentialled officials.
insights.locator: In December 2024, Putin again invoked the idea of a new elite
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Almost 44,000 people have applied to regional veteran programmes since 2024 with nearly 4,500 admitted — a roughly 10% acceptance rate, versus 0.26% federally — and around 1,200 admitted remain in a deferred pool because they are still deployed.
insights.so_what: The regional channel is where the volume is; the deferred pool is a queue of future officials that keeps growing while the war continues.
insights.locator: According to official regional figures, almost 44,000 people have applied
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Regional enrolment shows no statistically significant relationship with casualties or socioeconomic indicators; the ten highest per-capita enrolling large regions had 8.2 confirmed military deaths per 10,000 residents versus a 9.05 national rate, meaning governors' political incentives, not war losses, set the scale.
insights.so_what: Kills the intuitive read that veteran politics is strongest where the war hurt most — it is strongest where governors need to prove loyalty to Moscow.
insights.locator: There is no statistically significant relationship between enrolment
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: An estimated 170,000-400,000 people have already returned from the war, and the Kremlin is delegating their reintegration to regions without extra resources, so regional systems for employment, rehabilitation and social support are unlikely to cope with a larger demobilisation wave.
insights.so_what: Expect localised unrest, veteran crime and repression as the visible symptom of Russian demobilisation — destabilising but unlikely to threaten the federal regime directly.
insights.locator: An estimated 170,000–400,000 people have already come back
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Veteran-liaison roles account for 44% of regional appointments versus 18% federally, and 31% of all regional appointments went to newly created or repurposed veteran-support posts, showing regions are building a buffer bureaucracy to manage discontent rather than filling real vacancies.
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a genuine elite pipeline (federal) from a social-control instrument (regional) — do not treat headline veteran-appointment counts as one thing.
insights.locator: veteran-liaison roles appear to account for 44% of regional appointments
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: The Kremlin's likely response to veteran discontent is to sustain a split between a small number of rewarded “good” veterans and a repressed majority whose grievance stays nationalist, militarist and revanchist and could outlast Putin.
insights.so_what: Post-war Russia scenarios should assume an angry armed constituency that is anti-government but not pro-Western — liberalisation is not the default outcome of demobilisation.
insights.locator: The Kremlin’s response to this is likely to preserve the distinction
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

themes.theme: Duma 2026: a managed, deliberately diluted veteran bloc

insights.claim: Of 546 self-declared war participants entering United Russia's 2026 Duma primaries, only 83 reached the ballot and roughly 47 are projected to win, so the next State Duma will contain no more than about 50 veterans — around 11% of its 450 seats.
insights.so_what: Sets the actual size of the parliamentary war lobby: loud but far short of a controlling bloc.
insights.locator: Based on list positions and the dynamics in single-member districts
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Kremlin-aligned experts' expectations for veteran Duma representation fell from 40% of seats in 2025 to 20% and then lower still, a retreat that likely reflects presidential-administration fear that a large veteran bloc would be harder to manage than existing factions.
insights.so_what: The regime is rationing its own militarist constituency — evidence that the Kremlin sees veterans as a control problem, not just an asset.
insights.locator: In 2025, Kremlin-aligned experts predicted that veterans could take 40%
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: At least 31 of United Russia's 83 veteran Duma candidates are unlikely to have seen combat, mostly claiming status through officials' “volunteer battalions” that investigations found generally operate far from the frontline.
insights.so_what: Headline counts of “veterans in power” overstate the real combat cohort; nominal veterans are careerists adopting a new credential, much as officials once joined technocrat programmes.
insights.locator: Analysis of their biographies found that at least 31 of the 83
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Some 427 of the 463 war-linked contenders excluded from United Russia's final slate had probably seen combat, and even a roughly 25% electoral bonus for veteran candidates could not overcome the party's managed selection.
insights.so_what: The party machine actively filters real combatants out — a rare quantified look at how Russian candidate selection overrides voter preference.
insights.locator: The filtering out of combat veterans began at the primary stage
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Enrolment in Time of Heroes is the single clearest marker of favourable electoral prospects: 19 of the programme's 28 Duma candidates are projected to win (68%) versus 51% for other veteran candidates.
insights.so_what: Programme membership is the tradeable credential inside the Russian system — a usable screen for identifying rising officials.
insights.locator: Enrolment in Time of Heroes is the clearest marker
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Veterans hold only 6-10% of seats in consequential regional parliaments and regional-capital councils, with outliers in high-casualty and annexed territories such as Tuva (16%), Komi (17%) and occupied Sevastopol (21%).
insights.so_what: Claims of thousands of veteran deputies mostly refer to unpaid municipal seats — real legislative penetration is still modest.
insights.locator: The same pattern appears in regional legislatures
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Mixing officials who briefly donned khaki with career soldiers across institutions dilutes any “combat brotherhood” and is a deliberate design choice to stop veterans coalescing into a coherent political bloc.
insights.so_what: Explains why a Russian veterans' party is unlikely in the near term — and why the risk shows up only when these people are concentrated, as in the Duma.
insights.locator: Mixing officials who have briefly donned khaki with career soldiers
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: The Kremlin's caution is historically grounded: Lev Rokhlin tried to mobilise officers against Yeltsin, Igor Strelkov went from 2014 war hero to imprisoned critic, and Wagner's 2023 mutiny exposed the risk of an armed network with its own loyalties.
insights.so_what: Precedent for why loyal veterans are a recurring source of elite instability in Russia — the tail risk is internal, not electoral.
insights.locator: The Kremlin has reason for such caution
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

themes.theme: Implications for Europe and the post-Putin transition

insights.claim: A summer 2026 journalistic count puts more than 1,300 formally recognised veterans in Russian government bodies, rising rapidly year by year, making the phenomenon too large to dismiss as Kremlin PR.
insights.so_what: The scale threshold at which veteran integration becomes an institutional fact European planners must price in.
insights.locator: The latest journalistic count, from summer 2026
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: The cadre shift indicates Moscow is staffing the state for a prolonged period of active conflict, and increasingly damaging Ukrainian strikes during 2026 appear to have strengthened rather than weakened Putin's resolve to continue.
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing a near-term negotiated end to the war; deep strikes on Russia are provoking retaliation, not compromise.
insights.quote: There is little to suggest Putin is likely to end the war.
insights.locator: This cadre shift forms part of the wider normalisation of war
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: The veteran cohort's real significance emerges over the next 4-6 years as today's mid-ranking appointees rise into a constituency whose careers depend on preserving the war as an affirmative political myth, narrowing the scope for normalisation after a ceasefire or leadership change.
insights.so_what: A structural reason why sanctions relief and re-engagement with Russia may stay politically blocked in Moscow even after the fighting stops.
insights.locator: These will emerge over the next 4-6 years
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Despite louder militarist rhetoric from the new elite, the bark of Russian elite rhetoric is likely to remain worse than its bite, as shown by Medvedev's repeated nuclear warnings, Patrushev's prediction that Ukraine would cease to exist in 2025 and SVR false-flag claims that never materialised.
insights.so_what: Trade Russian escalation headlines against observable force posture and operational preparations, not statements — the statements are a market-moving noise source with a poor hit rate.
insights.quote: Still, the bark of elite rhetoric is likely to remain worse than its bite.
insights.locator: Stay cool in the face of sharpening rhetoric
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: An organised veteran faction in the Duma could gain weight without a formal caucus — through joint legislation, coordinated campaigns and mutual support on appointments — bargaining collectively for budgets and privileges while staying loyal to the Kremlin.
insights.so_what: A new rent-seeking interest group inside the Russian budget: expect sustained pressure on veteran benefits and military-adjacent spending lines.
insights.locator: A formal veterans caucus would not be necessary
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: During an eventual Russian transition an organised veteran faction would strengthen hardliners against comparatively pragmatic technocrats such as Mikhail Mishustin and cautiously loyal tycoons such as Andrey Melnichenko.
insights.so_what: Names the specific pragmatist bloc whose relative standing is the variable to watch for any future Russia-West de-escalation trade.
insights.locator: Such a more organised fraction would strengthen the position
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: Russia's ideological campaign has repeatedly failed with younger citizens — student recruitment into new drone forces relied on large payments and university pressure and eventually failed, while removing the peace-campaigning Yabloko party from the 2026 election triggered an unusually young wave of protest and detentions.
insights.so_what: Identifies a genuine limit to Russian militarisation: the state has bought compliance but not belief among the under-30s in large cities.
insights.locator: The broader ideological campaign developed in Russia since 2022
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin

insights.claim: European governments should keep educational and professional mobility routes open to Russians still inside the country — using remote or third-country selection and vetting — even after the Kremlin designated Germany's DAAD an “undesirable organisation”.
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost policy lever European states are currently abandoning; its reversal would be an early sign of a differentiated Russia strategy.
insights.locator: European governments should make use of this by widening educational
insights.speaker: Mikhail Komin
